subject: Archaeology
title: Ceramic Analysis: Stories in Pots
description: A quick win: understand Ceramic Analysis: Stories in Pots.

hook.text: Pottery is the most common find on most archaeological sites — and one of the most informative.

buildup.text: Clay composition reveals where a pot was made. Decoration and shape reveal when and by whom it was crafted.

discovery.text: Chemical analysis can match a pot to a specific clay source, proving trade routes that stretched hundreds of miles.

twist.text: Residue analysis detects what was inside. Traces of wine, olive oil, and even chocolate have been found.

climax.text: The oldest known chocolate was found inside a 3,900-year-old pot in Mesoamerica — 1,500 years before the Maya.

punchline.text: A broken pot is never just a broken pot. The clay, the shape — everything speaks.

quiz.question: What can residue analysis of ancient pottery reveal?
options: The exact recipe used to make the pot's clay
What was stored inside — wine, oil, milk, and even chocolate
The temperature at which the kiln was fired

details.summary: Pottery is the most common artifact at post-Neolithic archaeological sites. Ceramic analysis examines clay composition, temper, firing temperature, shape, and decoration to reconstruct trade networks, cooking practices, cultural identity, and technological development across thousands of years.
details.whyItMatters: Because pottery is nearly indestructible and stylistically varied, it serves as the backbone of archaeological dating and cultural identification. A trained ceramicist can date a site from a single potsherd.
takeaways: Pottery is the most common artifact at most archaeological sites
Clay composition and temper reveal where pots were manufactured
Style changes in pottery provide reliable dating frameworks

faq.question: What can a single potsherd tell an archaeologist?
faq.answer: The clay composition indicates where it was made. The temper type reveals manufacturing traditions. Shape and decoration place it in a cultural and chronological framework. Residue analysis can identify what was cooked or stored inside. A single fragment contains multiple data streams.

faq.question: How does pottery help establish trade networks?
faq.answer: When pots made from clay in one region appear at distant sites, they document trade connections. Chemical fingerprinting through techniques like neutron activation analysis or portable XRF matches pottery to specific clay sources, mapping exchange routes across regions.
